Does Alberta’s human rights law cover discrimination when someone is trying to rent a place to live?​A landlord who refuses to rent to someone because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression is committing a crime. The Alberta Human Rights Act covers discrimination when someone is trying to rent a place to live. If you believe you have been discriminated against when trying to rent a place to live, you can make a complaint to the Alberta Human Rights Commission. In the case of Vriend v. Alberta, the Supreme Court of Canada said that sexual orientation should be added to the list of characteristics protected from discrimination under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. After this ruling, Alberta added sexual orientation to section 4 of the Alberta Human Rights Act. Section 4 of the Act now protects Albertans from discrimination based on race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, gender identity, gender expression, physical disability, mental disability, age, ancestry, place of origin, marital status, parent-child relationship, family status, source of income, and sexual orientation. It is against the law for landlords to discriminate against renters because of any of these characteristics. For more information about housing discrimination, see the Alberta Human Rights Commission’s information sheet on housing and human rights. The information sheet also includes a link to information about human rights issues related to rental housing and issues experienced by people who are homeless.
